forces: Flute, solo violin, obbligato harpsichord, strings and continuo
performers: Advent Chamber Orchestra; Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord
intro: In the first movement, Allegro, of Bach’s Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050, flute, violin and harpsichord share the solo passages. Bach wrote out sixty-five bars for the harpsichord unaccompanied.

sections.label: A · Opening ritornello, strings, D major
sections.mNote: The violins play the opening ritornello; the flute rests.

sections.label: C · Soloists in minor keys
sections.mNote: Keyboard runs between the string ritornellos.

sections.label: D · String ritornello in D major
sections.mNote: The violins play the refrain again in the home key.

sections.label: E · Flute and violin over keyboard
sections.mNote: The flute and violin play above the harpsichord’s running notes.

sections.label: F · Harpsichord passagework and string ritornellos
sections.mNote: The harpsichord’s solo passages become longer.

sections.label: Cadenza · Harpsichord alone
sections.mNote: Two hands play every part for sixty-five bars.

sections.label: A · Strings, opening refrain in D major
sections.mNote: The opening D major refrain closes the movement.

relations.label: The opening ritornello returns
relations.basis: The opening and final ritornellos frame the solo episodes and written-out cadenza; the section map places the final tutti near 568 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.954, sustained 17 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 566.5 s (cache/form/bach-brandenburg-5-allegro.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening ritornello, strings
cues.text: The two violin parts play the same brisk D major refrain over a moving bass. The flute is silent. This refrain is the ritornello, the music the strings bring back between the soloists’ excursions.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871), I, opening eight bars. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ed/IMSLP02043-BWV1050.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute, violin and harpsichord soloists
cues.text: Flute and violin exchange short phrases, and the harpsichord’s right hand joins them while its left hand plays the bass. Bach wrote the keyboard’s solo passages out in full, alternating with figured-bass accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, from bar 9; the harpsichord alternates written-out solo passages with figured-bass accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Arrest at Weimar, 1717
cues.text: In 1717 Bach signed a contract with Prince Leopold at Köthen before he had permission to leave Weimar. His employer would not accept his resignation and had him confined for a month. He was released and dismissed in December, and took up the post at Köthen.

cues.title: Harpsichord cadenza, 1721 version
cues.text: An earlier version gives the harpsichord an eighteen-bar solo. In the score dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1721, Bach expanded it to sixty-five bars. The flute and violin have no solo of comparable length.
cues.evidence: Comparison of BWV 1050.1 and BWV 1050.2, including the expanded cadenza. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5

cues.title: Visit to Berlin, March 1719
cues.text: In March 1719 Bach travelled from Köthen to Berlin to collect a new harpsichord for Prince Leopold’s court. He probably played for Margrave Christian Ludwig on that visit. In the 1721 dedication of these concertos Bach recalled doing so “a couple of years ago”.
cues.evidence: Netherlands Bach Society, notes on BWV 1050: Bach’s dedication preface and the March 1719 Berlin visit to receive a new harpsichord for Köthen. https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1050

cues.title: Collegium Musicum, Leipzig, from 1729
cues.text: From 1729 Bach directed Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum, whose weekly concerts at Café Zimmermann moved outdoors in summer. The programmes included his orchestral suites and his violin and harpsichord concertos, and Bach appeared in them as a keyboard player.

cues.title: Harpsichord solo, bars 154–218
cues.text: The other instruments stop. The harpsichord keeps the bass and plays increasingly elaborate figures above it. The solo is written out in full in the score, down to its fastest notes, and the orchestra rests for sixty-five bars.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bars 154–218. The formal boundaries are tabulated by San Francisco Conservatory: https://sfcm.edu/sites/default/files/sfcm-theory/analysis_lectures/21_concerto/brandenburg_5_chart.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harpsichord cadenza
cues.text: Bach gives the keyboard broken chords and rapid alternations of the kind a concerto would usually give to a solo violinist. In the unaccompanied cadenza the left hand plays the bass notes while the right hand moves above it.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, extended cadenza; the transfer of violin techniques to the keyboard is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Final ritornello, strings
cues.text: At bar 219, after the long keyboard solo, the strings return with the ritornello in D major, with the violins in unison. The harpsichord goes back to accompanying, and the flute rests to the end, as it did at the opening.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bar 219 to the end, p. 148: string ritornello, flute rests and harpsichord marked accomp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From opening refrain to first episode
transitions.from: A · Opening ritornello, strings, D major
transitions.how: The eight-bar string refrain closes in D major. Flute and solo violin then exchange phrases above the harpsichord’s bass, and the keyboard’s right hand joins their runs. The pulse is unchanged. The solo episode modulates to A major, and the next string refrain enters in that key.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bars 1–19; San Francisco Conservatory form chart: https://sfcm.edu/sites/default/files/sfcm-theory/analysis_lectures/21_concerto/brandenburg_5_chart.pdf

transitions.title: Harpsichord solo before the ritornello
transitions.from: F · Harpsichord passagework and string ritornellos
transitions.how: The other players stop, and the harpsichord plays both the bass and the upper parts. Its solo prolongs A major, the dominant of D. Sequences and broken chords follow, in steadily smaller note values, until the strings return with their refrain.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bars 154–218; dominant function and cadenza boundaries in the San Francisco Conservatory form chart.

transitions.title: Cadenza into the final D major ritornello
transitions.to: A · Strings, opening refrain in D major
transitions.how: The harpsichord’s last running figures lead into the opening violin refrain in D major, which returns as the final ritornello from bar 219. The keyboard changes to accompaniment, marked accomp., and the string basses return beneath the violins. The flute rests through the closing refrain.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, p. 148: end of the cadenza and final ritornello, from bar 219.

source.title: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050, full score (Bach-Gesellschaft, 1871)
source.locator: I. Allegro, printed pp. 127–148: flute, solo violin, harpsichord, ripieno violin, viola, cello and violone. The solo keyboard cadenza occupies bars 154–218. The flute rests in the opening and closing string refrains.

timeline.note: Solo and ripieno violins play the opening refrain. The flute rests while the strings and harpsichord supply the bass.
Flute, violin and harpsichord begin their exchanges. The ripieno strings join them for the returning refrains.
Flute and violin trade phrases above the harpsichord’s quick notes and the accompanying strings.
The strings return to their ritornello while the harpsichord’s runs grow longer.
The harpsichord plays alone through the cadenza, supplying bass, chords and fast upper lines.
The strings return with the opening refrain. The harpsichord accompanies; the flute is silent.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
